extracted.intended_audience: USPTO examiners and patent practitioners evaluating §101 patent eligibility
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for applying the Alice/Mayo two-part test (Step 2A Prong Two and Step 2B) to determine whether claims that recite judicial exceptions are integrated into a practical application or contain an inventive concept sufficient for patent eligibility under 35 U.S.C. §101.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particular Treatment and Prophylaxis integration (Step 2A Prong Two)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim reciting a judicial exception is not directed to the judicial exception if it also recites additional element(s) demonstrating that the claim as a whole integrates the exception into a practical application; one way to demonstrate such integration is when the additional elements apply or use the recited judicial exception to effect a particular treatment or prophylaxis for a disease or medical condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that use the judicial exception to effect a particular treatment or prophylaxis meaningfully limit the claim by going beyond generally linking the exception to a technological environment and thus are eligible at Step 2A. See Vanda (method of treating patients where dosing depended on genotype) as an example of eligibility. Examples of treatment/prophylaxis include acupuncture, administration of medication, dialysis, organ transplants, phototherapy, physiotherapy, radiation therapy, surgery, immunization steps that lower disease risk (Classen). The limitation must affirmatively recite an action that effects a particular treatment or prophylaxis (e.g., 'administering amazonic acid to a patient'); mere intended use, prescribing without actual use, or field-of-use language (e.g., 'pharmaceutical composition', 'feed dispenser operable to dispense') do not integrate the exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particularity or Generality of the Treatment or Prophylaxis
rubrics_metrics.description: The treatment or prophylaxis limitation must be 'particular,' i.e., specifically identified so that it does not encompass all applications of the judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Particular limitations integrate the judicial exception into a practical application (example: 'administering a lower than normal dosage of a beta blocker medication to a patient identified as having the poor metabolizer genotype'). Generic instructions (example: 'administering a suitable medication to a patient') are not particular and therefore do not integrate the exception. Examiners may evaluate related considerations such as mere instructions to apply an exception and field-of-use/technological-environment considerations (see MPEP § 2106.05(f), § 2106.05(h)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relationship significance between limitation and exception
rubrics_metrics.description: The treatment or prophylaxis limitation must have more than a nominal or insignificant relationship to the judicial exception(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the recited treatment meaningfully uses the recited law of nature/exception to achieve the therapeutic/prophylactic effect. Example: 'treating a patient having blood glucose >250 mg/dl with insulin' significantly relates to the correlation and integrates the law of nature; 'treating with aspirin' has at best a nominal connection and does not meaningfully apply the exception. Consider also the insignificant extra-solution activity and field-of-use factors (see MPEP § 2106.05(g) and § 2106.05(h)).

rubrics_metrics.name: No extra-solution activity or mere field-of-use
rubrics_metrics.description: The treatment or prophylaxis limitation must impose meaningful limits on the judicial exception and cannot be extra-solution activity or merely a field-of-use limitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the allegedly therapeutic step is performed merely to gather data or as a necessary precursor for the abstract/exception-focused activity, it is extra-solution activity and does not integrate the exception (example: administering vaccines to collect data for analysis). Conversely, a later step that applies the analysis to alter therapy for a second group (thus reducing risk) applies the exception to a practical treatment and integrates it. Cross-reference insignificant extra-solution activity and field-of-use considerations (MPEP § 2106.05(g), § 2106.05(h)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Affirmative recitation requirement for treatment/prophylaxis limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: To qualify under the treatment/prophylaxis consideration, the claim must affirmatively recite an action that effects a particular treatment or prophylaxis for a disease or medical condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positive examples: steps like 'administering amazonic acid to a patient' or 'administering a course of plasmapheresis to a patient' are affirmative. Non-positive examples that fail to integrate the exception include mere intended uses ('prescribing a topical steroid' — does not require actual use) or labels/field-of-use statements ('pharmaceutical composition', 'feed dispenser operable to dispense a mineral supplement').

rubrics_metrics.name: Search for an inventive concept (Step 2B)
rubrics_metrics.description: An inventive concept cannot be furnished by the unpatentable law of nature (or natural phenomenon or abstract idea) itself; it is furnished by additional element(s) recited in the claim beyond the judicial exception that ensure the claim as a whole amounts to significantly more than the judicial exception itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The search for an inventive concept asks what else is in the claims beyond the exception. Courts and MPEP instruct that an inventive concept must be an element or combination of elements sufficient to ensure the claim amounts to significantly more than the exception. See Alice, Genetic Technologies, RecogniCorp. The presence of additional elements must be evaluated to determine whether they constitute significantly more than the judicial exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate additional elements individually and in combination
rubrics_metrics.description: Additional elements must be considered both individually and as an ordered combination to determine whether they amount to significantly more than the judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consideration in combination is particularly important because elements that are conventional individually may, in a non-conventional arrangement, provide an inventive concept (see Rapid Litigation Mgmt. v. CellzDirect; BASCOM). The Supreme Court emphasizes that claims must be considered as a whole (Diamond v. Diehr; Alice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive concept inquiry is distinct from novelty/obviousness (§§102/103)
rubrics_metrics.description: The search for an inventive concept under §101 is separate from inquiries under §§102 and 103; novelty or non-obviousness of elements is not determinative of §101 eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conflate conventionality with novelty or obviousness. Lack of novelty under §102 or obviousness under §103 does not necessarily indicate that additional elements are well-understood, routine, conventional for §101 purposes. See Mayo rejecting substitution of §§102/103 inquiries and cases such as Intellectual Ventures I v. Symantec, Synopsys v. Mentor Graphics, BASCOM.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration: Improvements to functioning of a computer
rubrics_metrics.description: An improvement to the functioning of a computer (e.g., modifying conventional protocols to produce a novel effect) can qualify as significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: DDR Holdings (modification of hyperlink protocol to dynamically produce a dual-source hybrid webpage) — such improvements have been found to supply an inventive concept. See MPEP § 2106.05(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration: Improvements to other technology or technical field
rubrics_metrics.description: An improvement to a non-computer technology or the technical field can supply an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Diamond v. Diehr (modifying rubber-molding processes with a thermocouple to monitor temperature and reduce under-/over-curing). See MPEP § 2106.05(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration: Applying the judicial exception by use of a particular machine
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying the judicial exception with or by use of a particular machine (with specific structure) can contribute to an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: using a Fourdrinier machine arranged in a particular way to optimize speed while maintaining quality (Eibel Process Co.). See MPEP § 2106.05(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration: Effecting a transformation of a particular article
rubrics_metrics.description: A process that effects a transformation or reduction of a particular article to a different state or thing can amount to significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: transforming raw, uncured synthetic rubber into precision-molded products (Diehr). See MPEP § 2106.05(c).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration: Adding specific limitations or unconventional arrangements
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding a specific limitation other than well-understood, routine, conventional activity in the field, or adding unconventional steps that confine the claim to a particular useful application, can supply an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: BASCOM — a non-conventional and non-generic arrangement of known components (installation of a filtering tool at a specific remote location with customizable filtering features) constituted significantly more. See MPEP § 2106.05(d).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration: Other meaningful limitations beyond mere technological environment linkage
rubrics_metrics.description: Other meaningful limitations that do more than generally link use of the judicial exception to a particular technological environment can constitute significantly more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: an immunization step that integrates an abstract idea of data comparison into a specific immunization process lowering later disease risk (Classen). See MPEP § 2106.05(e).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations that are insufficient to constitute significantly more
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain types of additions to a claim have been found to be insufficient to qualify as an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples identified by the courts include: (i) adding the words 'apply it' or mere instructions to implement an abstract idea on a computer (Alice); (ii) appending well-understood, routine, conventional activities specified at a high level of generality (generic computer functions); (iii) adding insignificant extra-solution activity (mere data gathering) (CyberSource); and (iv) generally linking the abstract idea to a particular technological environment or field-of-use (Bilski, Parker v. Flook). See MPEP §§ 2106.05(f)-(h).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tangibility/physicality of additional elements is not determinative
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere physical or tangible implementation of an exception is not, by itself, an inventive concept; conversely, non-physical or intangible elements are not automatically disqualifying.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The fact that a computer is a tangible machine is 'beside the point' if the claimed computer performs only conventional, generic functions (Alice). Physical steps alone (e.g., DNA amplification/analysis) do not necessarily provide sufficient inventive concept (Genetic Technologies). Conversely, improvements not defined by reference to physical components can still be eligible (Enfish; McRO — intangible result that improved technological process). Consider the substance and how elements operate together, not mere physicality.

rubrics_metrics.name: How courts apply the second-part analysis in practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts identify additional claim elements, evaluate them individually for whether they are well-understood/routine/conventional, and then evaluate them as an ordered combination to determine if the combination yields significantly more than the judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alice: Court identified additional elements (computer functions/hardware), found each was well-understood/routine/conventional, and determined that the ordered combination added nothing significantly more. BASCOM: district court recognized additional elements as generic when viewed individually, but the Federal Circuit emphasized the need to assess the combination, which produced an inventive concept in that arrangement. Use these steps as a template for Step 2B analysis (identify additional elements, analyze individually, analyze in combination).
